steps.title: Prepare Electrolyte Solution
steps.instruction: Determine the electrolyte composition (LiFSI:DMC molar ratio 1.0:1.6) and calculate the required amounts; weigh 0.5 mL DMC (sufficient for 20 cells) and the appropriate mass of LiFSI in an Ar‑filled glove box; add ~0.05 mL extra DMC to compensate for solvent loss that reduces the actual ratio to ~1.0:1.45; mix by vortex or hand shaking at 25 °C until the salt dissolves (≈10 min). Store the electrolyte at 25 °C and use within 1 month.

steps.title: Prepare Battery Materials
steps.instruction: Select SS 2025‑type coin cells with 0.5 mm SS spacers; cut NCM523 cathode (96 % active material, 2 % conductive additive, 2 % binder) into 13 mm disks (area capacity 2.7 mAh cm⁻²); cut Cu foil anodes into 16–17 mm disks; cut PE separator and Al foil (cathode current collector) into 19 mm disks; dry all components (vacuum 24 h or glove box <0.1 ppm H₂O for 1 week at 25 °C) before transferring into the glove box.

steps.title: Prepare Diluent Extraction Solution
steps.instruction: Choose deuterated DMSO‑d₆ as the diluent; add maleic acid (MA) as titrant at 100 mM and Cr(acac)₃ as relaxation enhancer at 0.5 mM; weigh the required amounts and transfer 40 mL DMSO‑d₆ into the container in the glove box; shake at 25 °C until the solution is clear (≈5 min). Store at 25 °C and use within 1 month.

steps.title: Extract Electrolyte from Cells
steps.instruction: Wash the die of the coin‑cell unsealing machine and cell cases with dimethoxyethane (DME) for 10 min; pipette 2 mL of the prepared extraction solution into a container (diameter > 20 mm); disassemble cycled cells with hydraulic crimpers inside the Ar glove box (≈1 min) and immediately place the opened cells into the container, then seal (<3 s); wait ~5 min for Li‑metal titration (observe blackish deposition on Cu foil); shake the sealed container on an automatic shaker for 40 min (≈45 min total) ensuring thorough mixing; let the mixture rest for an additional 40 min; add 20 µL of internal reference (DCBF) into each NMR tube (10 min); transfer 0.6 mL of the mixed solution into the same NMR tubes (10 min).

steps.title: Process NMR Data and Fit ETNs
steps.instruction: Using JEOL Delta, correct chemical shifts with TMS (¹H) and DCBF (¹⁹F) (10 min); correct phase and baseline (10 min); extract and integrate peak areas automatically, keeping the same integration width for each signal (20 min); if peaks overlap, perform Voigt‑function fitting as needed. Calculate irreversible capacity of the anode‑free cells: (a) nth accumulated deposition capacity = Σ₁ⁿ charge capacity; (b) nth accumulated irreversible capacity = 1st charge capacity – nth discharge capacity (20 min). Compute relative component contents with n_Ai/Z_i = I_Ai¹H/NA¹H·IR_i¹H/NIR¹H·IZ_iX/NZ·X·IR_iX/NIRX (5 min). Compute absolute contents using n_Zi = (I_ZiX/NZ·X·IR_iX/NIRX) / (ID_i¹H/IR_i¹H·ID_blank¹H/IR_blank¹H) × (m₃·M_IR·V₁/V₂), where NDMC¹H=6, NDCBF¹H=3, NFSI¹⁹F=2, NMA¹H=2, NDCBF¹⁹F=3, m₃=32.9 µg, M_IR=215.00 g mol⁻¹, V₁=40 mL, V₂=0.60 mL (5 min). Determine absolute loss Δn = n_Zi – n_Z0; calculate irreversible capacity from inactive Li: irre.capacity = Δn_titrant·F (F = Faraday constant, 26.8 mAh mol⁻¹). Repeat the entire data‑collection steps for at least two C‑rates (≈2 days). Fit electron‑transfer numbers (ETNs) by multiple linear regression in MATLAB: input solvent consumption (X), anion consumption (Y), and irreversible capacity (Z) and fit Z = (z₁·X + z₂·Y)·F (30 min).

description: In non-aqueous secondary batteries, the electrolyte decomposition reactions at the anode/electrolyte interface are considered to be the most important and complex phenomenon.2 Electrolyte decomposition reactions lead to irreversible capacity decay and the formation of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), which dictates the performance and stability of the anode. However, because of the complexity of simultaneous reactions of multiple components of the electrolyte and the interference of inevitably formed inactive lithium,3 it is hard to accurately measure the change of different electrolyte components and assign the corresponding electron consumption. In the battery community, qNMR has been proven to be a powerful tool to investigate the electrolyte composition and its evolution upon cycling in various systems.4,5,6,7,8 Herein, the procedure of qNMR for electrolyte quantification and the recently developed electron transfer numbers (ETNs) fitting method are documented and elucidated. Normally, the electrolyte should be prepared beforehand, though the commercialized electrolyte with known components can be used as well. The deuterated diluent that contains titrant should also be prepared. Moreover, the software for quantitative NMR (qNMR) data processing and multivariate regression analysis is also necessary, which are JEOL Delta and MATLAB in this protocol. As for the battery configuration, the anode-free battery, namely a battery without lithium metal, should be used to reflect the total irreversible capacity loss of the anode.9 Besides, multiple samples at different C-rates are required for the subsequent apparent ETN fitting. The protocol below describes the specific steps for using coin cells with dimethyl carbonate (DMC)-based high-concentration electrolyte (HCE). We have also used this protocol in anode-free pouch cells and with other types of electrolyte.1
